text: If for some reason you wanted to draw everything that exists on the same chart, a good way would be to use the log of mass and size.
Do that and you notice that almost everything falls along this diagonal lines and it's not hard to see why.
In the metric system, one milliliter of water weighs one gram and fills a cube exactly one centimeter wide. Most things are in cubes though, so we will measure everything as if they were a ball.
On a log chart that only shifts things by a tiny bit to the right, you won't even notice.
Now make every side ten times longer, ten centimeters. On a log chart that's one unit to the right, but the volume grows a thousand times to one liter and one liter of water weights one kilogram.
That's three units up on the max axis.
Do it again, 10 times the size, and you get 1 ,000 times the mass, one ton.

All of these will draw a diagonal line, the density of water. Everything to the left is, by definition, denser than water, so it sinks. Here we have things made of stone and metal. Anything to the right will float.

In the same way, you can draw a line for the density of air at one atmosphere on Earth. It separates things heavier than air from things lighter than air. And as the name says, here are the lighter than air aircrafts, balloons and zeppelins.
Most animals though, live in a much narrower band. That's because we are mostly made of water. Some of us are a little denser than others.
The hippo, for example, can't actually swim. It just bounces along the riverbed.
we will see heavier animals like the elephants. The largest animal ever on land was the Argentinosaur, but the largest animal ever is still around and that's the blue whale.
But if we talk about the largest tree, then that's a sequoia, which is much bigger.
Past living things, and we get to engineering. Notice that the Eiffel Tower is surprisingly light for its size.

That's because we're also counting all the space inside it. Its whole shape, air included, is about one and a half million cubic meters. Leave out the arch and the gaps and it shrinks about five times.
The iron alone would fit in a cube 11 meters wide, which is denser than water and it would definitely sink.
In many ways the Eiffel Tower is kind of a fractal, how big it is depends on how close you look.
Then comes big rocks and big buildings and the Great Pyramid which is a little bit of both. Above that we have lakes and asteroids and then we arrive at small moons.

As we move up the line you notice objects becoming more spherical and less potato shaped. That's because until now the force holding matter in shape was the chemical bonds between the atoms. But now from this point on gravity it takes over and that's what shapes planets and it shapes them in many other ways neither mercury nor the moon has enough gravity to hold on to an atmosphere then as an earth do but not enough to keep the lightest gases hydrogen and helium and since most of the visible matter in the universe is made of those two once a planet can hold on to them it can grow into a gas
So, Earth lives in a kind of gravitational Goldilocks zone, just enough mass for its temperature to hold on to oxygen and nitrogen, not enough to hold on to hydrogen and helium.

You can see it on the chart, most of these dots stop following the rocky planets on the left and move to the right where planets are mostly gas. Saturn is actually less dense than water, roughly as dense as wood, and it would float like a log.

Then the trend suddenly stops. You can't get a planet much bigger than Jupiter. Objects 10 times, even 80 times more massive are still roughly Jupiter -sized. That's because the pressure in their core is so high that electrons are squeezed out of their atoms and they push back.
And more mass and the object get denser, not bigger.

And then right about brown dwarfs, there's a huge split. Some objects veer to the right and some veer to the left because now we are no longer talking about the story of ordinary matter. We are talking about life and death of stars.
